title: Strong local dephasing in Dicke superradiance
text:
Collective emission and independent-emitter decay can arise from the same collective jump operator. Strong local dephasing changes which total-spin sectors are occupied. Averaging the collective emission rate over their stationary distribution then gives a rate proportional to the number of excitations.
The calculation connects two continuous-time Markov chains: a fast birth–death process in total spin and a slow pure-death process in excitation number. The stationary distribution of the first determines the rates of the second.
This calculation originated as an appendix draft for our decoherence paper. It is presented here as a standalone derivation, with the Markov-chain connection made explicit. The paper studies the broader competition between collective emission, local dephasing, and spontaneous emission; this note isolates the limit of strong local dephasing without an additional spontaneous-emission channel.

title: Strong local dephasing in Dicke superradiance
text:
Model and conventions
Consider \(N\) identical two-level emitters, with \(\hbar=1\),
\[
J_-=\sum_{i=1}^N\sigma_-^{(i)},
\qquad
J_z=\sum_{i=1}^N s_z^{(i)},
\qquad
s_z^{(i)}=\frac12\left(\lvert e_i\rangle\langle e_i\rvert-\lvert g_i\rangle\langle g_i\rvert\right).
\]
The master equation is
\[
\dot\rho=\Gamma\mathcal D[J_-]\rho
+\xi\sum_{i=1}^N\mathcal D[s_z^{(i)}]\rho,
\qquad
\mathcal D[L]\rho=L\rho L^\dagger-\frac12\{L^\dagger L,\rho\}.
\]
Here \(\Gamma\) is the single-emitter population decay rate. With the spin-\(1/2\) convention for \(s_z\), dephasing alone damps a single-emitter optical coherence at rate \(\xi/2\). There is no drive, Hamiltonian, or additional local emission channel. The dephasing acts independently on each emitter.
We assume a permutationally invariant state diagonal in the Dicke basis, including the fully excited initial state. Let \(p_{S,M}\) be the probability in the total-spin sector \(S\) at inversion \(M\), summed over its multiplicity. The excitation number is \(n=N/2+M\). The allowed spins are \(S=|M|,|M|+1,\ldots,N/2\); this includes half-integer spins for odd \(N\).
The limiting statement below takes \(\xi/\Gamma\to\infty\) at fixed \(N\). The regime of interest is strong dephasing relative to the collective scale, \(\xi\gg N\Gamma\).

title: Strong local dephasing in Dicke superradiance
section: The fast Markov chain at fixed inversion
text:
The fast Markov chain at fixed inversion
Local dephasing preserves \(M\) and changes \(S\) by one. Its off-diagonal transition rates are
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{S,M}&=\xi\,
\frac{(S-M+1)(S+M+1)(N-2S)}{4(S+1)(2S+1)},\\
b_{S,M}&=\xi\,
\frac{(S-M)(S+M)(N+2S+2)}{4S(2S+1)},
\end{aligned}
\]
for \(S\to S+1\) and \(S\to S-1\), respectively. Transitions outside the allowed spin interval are absent: \(a_{N/2,M}=0\) and \(b_{|M|,M}=0\). At \(S=0\), the latter is set to zero without evaluating the quotient. These are the standard permutationally invariant dephasing rates in the convention above; see Shammah et al..
At fixed \(M\), dephasing therefore generates the birth–death equation
\[
\dot p_{S,M}
=a_{S-1,M}p_{S-1,M}+b_{S+1,M}p_{S+1,M}
-(a_{S,M}+b_{S,M})p_{S,M},
\]
with unavailable inflow terms omitted. Here “birth” and “death” refer to the spin coordinate, not to the excitation number. Dephasing emits no photons in this model.

title: Strong local dephasing in Dicke superradiance
section: Detailed balance and the stationary distribution
text:
Detailed balance and the stationary distribution
Write \(\pi_{S|M}\) for the normalized stationary distribution of this fast chain. Detailed balance on each adjacent pair requires
\[
a_{S-1,M}\pi_{S-1|M}=b_{S,M}\pi_{S|M}.
\]
Substituting the rates gives
\[
\frac{\pi_{S|M}}{\pi_{S-1|M}}
=\frac{(N-2S+2)(2S+1)}{(N+2S+2)(2S-1)}.
\]
The factors containing \(M\) cancel. This is also the ratio \(d_S/d_{S-1}\) of the spin-sector multiplicities
\[
\begin{aligned}
d_S
&=\binom{N}{N/2-S}-\binom{N}{N/2-S-1}\\
&=\frac{N!(2S+1)}{(N/2-S)!(N/2+S+1)!}.
\end{aligned}
\]
A binomial coefficient with a lower index outside \(0,\ldots,N\) is zero. Each copy of spin \(S\) contains exactly one state with a specified allowed \(M\). Consequently,
\[
\sum_{S=|M|}^{N/2}d_S
=\binom{N}{N/2+M},
\]
which also follows by telescoping the difference of binomial coefficients. Normalization gives
\[
\boxed{
\pi_{S|M}
=\frac{d_S}{\binom{N}{N/2+M}}
=\frac{(2S+1)(N/2-M)!(N/2+M)!}
{(N/2-S)!(N/2+S+1)!}.
}
\]
The distribution depends on \(M\) through its allowed support and normalization, even though the adjacent-spin ratio is independent of \(M\).
There is a direct interpretation. At fixed excitation number \(n\), the stationary state is the uniform mixture of all \(\binom{N}{n}\) product configurations with \(n\) excited emitters. Permutational invariance makes their diagonal weights equal, and local dephasing removes coherences between distinct configurations. Decomposing this mixture into spin sectors gives precisely the multiplicity weights above.

title: Strong local dephasing in Dicke superradiance
text:
Averaging the collective emission rate
Collective emission preserves \(S\) and lowers \(M\) by one, with rate
\[
c_{S,M}=\Gamma(S+M)(S-M+1)
=\Gamma\left[S(S+1)-M(M-1)\right].
\]
We need its average under \(\pi_{S|M}\). The uniform product-state mixture provides a short way to evaluate it. For any product configuration \(\lvert x\rangle\) with \(n\) excitations,
\[
\langle x|J_+J_-|x\rangle
=\sum_i\langle x|\sigma_+^{(i)}\sigma_-^{(i)}|x\rangle
=n.
\]
The cross terms with \(i\ne j\) have zero diagonal matrix element. Since \(J_+J_-\) has eigenvalue \(S(S+1)-M(M-1)\) in a Dicke state, this proves
\[
\sum_S\pi_{S|M}\left[S(S+1)-M(M-1)\right]
=\frac N2+M,
\]
or equivalently,
\[
\left\langle S(S+1)\right\rangle_M=\frac N2+M^2.
\]
The effective emission rate is therefore
\[
\boxed{
\overline c_M=\sum_S c_{S,M}\pi_{S|M}
=\Gamma\left(\frac N2+M\right)=\Gamma n.
}
\]
This is an exact stationary average for every finite \(N\). Its use as the dynamical rate requires the separation of dephasing and emission timescales.

title: Strong local dephasing in Dicke superradiance
section: Stochastic averaging: the slow Markov chain
text:
Stochastic averaging: the slow Markov chain
Let \(q_M=\sum_Sp_{S,M}\). Summing the full population equations over \(S\) cancels the dephasing terms and gives the exact identity
\[
\dot q_M
=\sum_S c_{S,M+1}p_{S,M+1}
-\sum_S c_{S,M}p_{S,M}.
\]
At finite \(\xi\), this is generally not a closed equation for \(q_M\): the emission rate depends on the unresolved spin distribution. In the fast-dephasing limit, that distribution relaxes between emissions,
\[
p_{S,M}\simeq\pi_{S|M}q_M,
\]
so the limiting marginal dynamics is
\[
\dot q_M
=\Gamma\left(\frac N2+M+1\right)q_{M+1}
-\Gamma\left(\frac N2+M\right)q_M.
\]
An emission initially leaves the spin distribution inherited from the preceding inversion slice. Fast dephasing then redistributes it according to the stationary distribution on the new slice. This repeated relaxation is the reason stationary averaging closes the slow dynamics.
In Markov-chain language, this is stochastic averaging, or adiabatic elimination of the fast coordinate. With column probability vectors, let \(Q_{\mathrm{em}}\) be the collective-emission generator, \(R\) sum over \(S\), and \(E\) lift a marginal to local equilibrium, \((Eq)_{S,M}=\pi_{S|M}q_M\). Then \(RE\) is the identity and the limiting generator is
\[
Q_{\mathrm{eff}}=R Q_{\mathrm{em}}E.
\]
In terms of excitation probabilities \(P_n=q_{n-N/2}\), this becomes
\[
\dot P_n=\Gamma(n+1)P_{n+1}-\Gamma nP_n,
\qquad
n\longrightarrow n-1\quad\text{at rate }\Gamma n.
\]
The inflow term is absent at \(n=N\), and \(n=0\) is absorbing. These are exactly the population equations for \(N\) independently decaying emitters. They contrast with the symmetric Dicke ladder’s rates \(\Gamma n(N-n+1)\), derived in the companion Markov-chain note.

title: Strong local dephasing in Dicke superradiance
text:
Consequence for the emission curve
Starting with all emitters excited, the limiting solution is binomial,
\[
P_n(t)=\binom{N}{n}
\bigl(e^{-\Gamma t}\bigr)^n
\bigl(1-e^{-\Gamma t}\bigr)^{N-n}.
\]
Thus the mean excitation number and photon emission rate are
\[
\langle n(t)\rangle=Ne^{-\Gamma t},
\qquad
I(t)=\Gamma\langle n(t)\rangle
=\Gamma N e^{-\Gamma t}.
\]
Strong local dephasing removes the collective burst. The emission channel remains collective, but the fast redistribution over spin sectors reduces its averaged rate to the independent-emitter value.

title: Strong local dephasing in Dicke superradiance
text:
Scope
The stationary distribution and averaged-rate identities above are exact. The reduced dynamical equation is exact in the infinite-dephasing limit at fixed \(N\); finite dephasing can retain correlations and deviations from independent decay, including during an initial fast relaxation if the starting state is not already equilibrated. No uniform finite-\(N\) error bound is asserted here.
Local dephasing is essential. Replacing the separate \(s_z^{(i)}\) channels by collective dephasing \(\mathcal D[J_z]\) does not redistribute total spin and does not produce this mechanism. The Markov description concerns the Dicke-diagonal population sector specified above; it does not by itself establish independence for every quantum observable or measurement scheme.

title: Dicke superradiance as a continuous-time Markov chain
text:
Dicke superradiance provides a useful bridge between open quantum systems and classical stochastic processes. For a state diagonal in the symmetric Dicke basis, collective decay is described exactly by a continuous-time Markov chain. Each emission removes one excitation; the time spent waiting for that emission is random.
For a specified initial excitation number, the sequence of states is fixed. The randomness lies in the waiting times.

title: Dicke superradiance as a continuous-time Markov chain
section: From the master equation to transition rates
text:
From the master equation to transition rates
Consider \(N\) identical two-level emitters with collective lowering operator \(J_- = \sum_{i=1}^N \sigma_-^{(i)}\) and master equation
\[
\dot\rho = \Gamma\,\mathcal D[J_-]\rho,
\qquad
\mathcal D[L]\rho = L\rho L^\dagger
-\frac12\left\{L^\dagger L,\rho\right\}.
\]
Here \(\Gamma>0\) is the single-emitter population decay rate. We assume collective decay only, with no drive or other loss channels, and restrict to the fully symmetric sector \(j=N/2\).
Let \(\lvert k\rangle=\lvert j=N/2,m=k-N/2\rangle\) denote the Dicke state with \(k\) excitations. The ladder matrix element is
\[
J_-\lvert k\rangle
=\sqrt{k(N-k+1)}\,\lvert k-1\rangle.
\]
A diagonal initial state, including the fully excited state, remains diagonal:
\[
\rho(t)=\sum_{k=0}^N p_k(t)\lvert k\rangle\langle k\rvert.
\]
Its populations obey
\[
\dot p_k=r_{k+1}p_{k+1}-r_kp_k,
\qquad
r_k=\Gamma k(N-k+1),
\]
where \(r_0=0\) and the inflow term is absent at \(k=N\).

title: Dicke superradiance as a continuous-time Markov chain
text:
A pure-death Markov chain
Introduce a classical random variable \(K_t\in\{0,1,\ldots,N\}\) for the number of remaining excitations. Its only allowed transition is
\[
k\longrightarrow k-1
\quad\text{at rate}\quad
r_k=\Gamma k(N-k+1).
\]
This is a pure-death process, with \(k=0\) an absorbing state. The correspondence is



Collective decay
Markov-chain description




\(k\) excitations
State \(K_t=k\)


Dicke population \(p_k(t)\)
Probability \(\Pr(K_t=k)\)


Photon emission
Transition \(k\to k-1\)


Population rate equations
Kolmogorov forward equation



A diagonal mixture corresponds to drawing the initial state \(K_0\) with probabilities \(p_k(0)\).
Using a column probability vector \(\boldsymbol p=(p_0,\ldots,p_N)^\mathsf T\), write
\[
\dot{\boldsymbol p}=Q\boldsymbol p,
\qquad
Q_{k-1,k}=r_k,\quad Q_{k,k}=-r_k
\quad (k=1,\ldots,N),
\]
with all remaining entries zero, including \(Q_{0,0}=0\). Each column sums to zero, expressing conservation of probability, and
\[
\boldsymbol p(t)=e^{Qt}\boldsymbol p(0).
\]
The quantum model determines the rates. Once these rates are known, the population evolution can be studied using the tools of finite-state Markov chains.

title: Dicke superradiance as a continuous-time Markov chain
section: Waiting times and the emission burst
text:
Waiting times and the emission burst
At level \(k>0\), the waiting time \(\tau_k\) until the next photon has survival probability
\[
\Pr(\tau_k>\tau)=e^{-r_k\tau},
\qquad
\mathbb E[\tau_k]=\frac{1}{r_k}.
\]
After the jump, the process starts a new exponential waiting time at level \(k-1\). The embedded discrete jump chain simply visits \(N,N-1,\ldots,0\) when initialized at full excitation. The holding times are independent exponentials, with a different rate at each level.
The fully excited state has rate \(r_N=\Gamma N\). Around the middle of the ladder, the rate is of order \(\Gamma N^2\), so a trajectory passes through these levels much faster. For comparison, independent emitters give a pure-death process with rates \(r_k=\Gamma k\).
The ensemble photon emission rate is
\[
I(t)=\mathbb E[r_{K_t}]
=\sum_{k=0}^N r_kp_k(t)
=-\frac{d}{dt}\mathbb E[K_t].
\]
This distinguishes the instantaneous rate at a particular level from the experimentally averaged emission curve, which also depends on the distribution of occupied levels.

title: Dicke superradiance as a continuous-time Markov chain
section: Two emitters: equal rates, different populations
text:
Two emitters: equal rates, different populations
For \(N=2\), both nonzero transition rates are equal:
\[
2\xrightarrow{\,2\Gamma\,}1\xrightarrow{\,2\Gamma\,}0.
\]
Starting in \(k=2\), the populations are
\[
p_2(t)=e^{-2\Gamma t},\qquad
p_1(t)=2\Gamma t\,e^{-2\Gamma t},\qquad
p_0(t)=1-(1+2\Gamma t)e^{-2\Gamma t}.
\]
The time of the second photon is the sum of two independent exponential waiting times with rate \(2\Gamma\), an Erlang distribution. The factor of \(t\) in \(p_1\) also illustrates why formulas that assume distinct decay rates need care: Dicke rates satisfy \(r_k=r_{N-k+1}\).

title: Dicke superradiance as a continuous-time Markov chain
text:
Exact sampling in Julia
A trajectory can be sampled by drawing the waiting time at each level. This is the single-channel version of a Gillespie jump simulation; it introduces no time-step discretization.
using Random

function dicke_chain(N::Integer; Γ = 1.0, rng = Random.default_rng())
    N >= 0 || throw(ArgumentError("N must be nonnegative"))
    Γ > 0 || throw(ArgumentError("Γ must be positive"))

    times = [0.0]
    excitations = [N]
    t = 0.0

    for k in N:-1:1
        rate = Γ * k * (N - k + 1)
        t += randexp(rng) / rate
        push!(times, t)
        push!(excitations, k - 1)
    end

    return (; times, excitations)
end

path = dicke_chain(10; rng = Xoshiro(42))
path.times[2:end] contains the photon emission times. Between successive times, the excitation number is constant; after the last emission it remains zero. Averaging the occupancy of each level over many such paths recovers \(p_k(t)\).

title: Dicke superradiance as a continuous-time Markov chain
text:
Scope of the correspondence
The classical process describes excitation populations and photon-counting trajectories for the diagonal states considered here. The quantum state contains additional structure: individual Dicke basis states are generally entangled, and the separability of a mixture requires a separate analysis. Coherences and other measurement schemes require their own descriptions.
